maintopic: RHODESIA-STATEMENT AS TO EXTENT OF EMBARGO

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: RHODESIA-STATEMENT AS TO EXTENT OF EMBARGO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps at this time I could deal with a question asked yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition concerning the effectiveness of oil sanctions against Rhodesia. To supplement what I said yesterday, I would confirm that while there have been a number of press reports about shipments of oil into Rhodesia, some referring to shipments from South Africa and others to shipments from the Portuguese territory of Mozambique, these reports refer, in addition to gasoline, to other petroleum products such as kerosene.
While there have been many reports of this kind, it appears that some of them are exaggerated. For obvious reasons it is difficult to arrive at an exact estimate of the quantities of gasoline now entering Rhodesia, but the reports the government has received indicate that the quantity reaching Rhodesia from outside is only part of the daily consumption, even under the stringent rationing now in effect. Despite the shipments of gasoline into Rhodesia the stocks of gasoline in that country, I am informed, are diminishing.
The hon. gentleman also asked about the amount of oil delivered to Zambia by the R.C.A.F. Up to March 21 the amount has been 3,475 tons of oil.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: RHODESIA-STATEMENT AS TO EXTENT OF EMBARGO
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether the question I have in mind will be regarded by the Prime Minister as improper; however, the question simply is this. On the basis of the latest information what are the expectations now in respect of the breakdown of the Smith administration by reason of the imposition of sanctions, particularly in connection with oil?

maintopic: RHODESIA-STATEMENT AS TO EXTENT OF EMBARGO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a
commonwealth committee in London which is following the application of the sanctions. I believe it is to meet very shortly, and we will get a report on the effectiveness of the sanctions as we have been able to determine that effectiveness. All I would like to say at this moment is that the sanctions are being effective, but their full effect is perhaps going to take longer to see than we had thought to be the case when we met in Nigeria a couple of months ago.

March 22, 1966



The house resumed, from Monday, March 21, consideration of the motion of Mr. Sharp for committee of supply, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Diefenbaker, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Douglas.

Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned last night I was asking the question which literally millions of Canadians are asking more and more urgently every day. I asked, what is the government going to do about the rising cost of living? Everyone wants to know, and everyone needs to know. We must have action to bring the cost of living into line with the incomes of the people in this country.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
The government may not like the idea of a prices review board as suggested by the leader of this party. Very well, let members opposite suggest and implement their own machinery for keeping prices within the range of Canadian family incomes. This is what must be done. What worries me, as it does a great many others in this house, is that so far there seems to be no realization on the other side of the house that inflation is now a major problem. It has been brushed aside. But this cannot be done any longer without there being serious consequences for Canada.
I touched last night at some length on the grave consequences to family health, wellbeing and human dignity across this country. But there are other consequences we must take into account. If the government persists in pretending that measures concerned with trade and other aspects of the economy will of themselves suffice to deal with the cost of living, hon. gentlemen opposite are in for a rude shock.
If this process of inflation is allowed to go on much longer, this steady rise in the cost of living month by month, and if the cost of food in particular continues to increase, every organized group in this country, including professional organizations, trade unions, and even pensioner groups to the extent that they can do so, will be bound to engage in an ever fiercer struggle to protect their living standards. This is inevitable. What will happen will be that the stronger ones will get their incomes increased while the weaker will be pushed down still further into insecurity and misery.
Increased, Cost of Living
As surely as the sun will rise tomorrow, we in parliament will have to find more and more money to boost pensions and allowances for those whose purchasing power has been driven down and who have no effective means of raising their own incomes. I think this process is a stupid thing and vicious thing. There is no end to it. The time has come when the government should face the fact that incomes in this country must bear a sensible relation to the cost of living.
We say that the problem of holding the cost of living steady, or at least the cost of household essentials, is one which must be faced. We have suggested one way in which a start could be made. There are other ways in which action could be taken. But the important thing is action. We are deluding ourselves if we believe that steps taken to deal with big industries in this country will lead eventually to benefits trickling down to those in low income groups. This has nothing to do with reality.
I urge the government now, before it is too late, to deal as a matter of urgency with the cost of living as it relates to the incomes of ordinary Canadian families. It is one of the most important problems that we face this session.

Mr. Speaker, before I proceed with my remarks this afternoon I should like to express agreement with much of what the hon. lady has just said. It has always been my contention and the contention of members of this party that most Canadians do want to better their lot in freedom in the economic sense. Many of the hon. lady's remarks reminded me of the fact that we cannot talk about political freedom unless at the same time we concern ourselves with economic freedom.
In years gone by, though perhaps we never admitted it, inflation during relatively good times was something we learned to live with. It might be remembered that in past years most modern governments in the western world considered inflation as something which was inevitable, something which confronted most governments, especially, as I say, in good times. However, I suggest that today modern governments fully realize that the question of inflation, the question of an excessive rise in the cost of living, is one which must be dealt with. Otherwise, serious difficulties arise at home and the prestige of our country is seriously handicapped abroad.

March 22, 1966
Increased Cost of Living
If confidence is lost in the nation's money, if confidence is lost in the Canadian dollar, much harm is done at home and our prestige abroad is greatly impaired. I am sure the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) and the government of the day will agree with this proposition.
At the outset of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, let me frankly admit that a solution to the problem of rising costs or excessive inflation in a Canadian context is not easy. In many ways we have no real precedents, no historical tools to serve us. Yet this is no excuse for a government to do nothing. A solution to the problem of inflation, a solution to the problem of rising costs, will need imagination, determination and a firm hand.
For this reason I, together with most members of the house, I feel sure, was appalled by the speech which the Minister of Finance made yesterday. What were we told of the government's plan to face a situation which the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) himself described in Toronto as a serious one? The speech of the minister and the speeches of his supporters up to now have convinced me that the government of the day has no real plans to face the problem of rising costs.
Yesterday afternoon, after my leader had spoken, the minister was apparently satisfied to indulge in some unseemly partisan bickering. He gave us a historical survey of the sins of a past administration. Never for a moment did he doff his partisan blinkers. I ask the house, did the minister speak of one concrete plan which the government is adopting to fight inflation and rising costs? Did he talk about one single achievement which the government has to its credit since it came to power a few years ago in terms of facing this problem? All our members who heard the minister yesterday and all who have heard from supporters of the government since must answer, no. I would say that while the minister may have great administrative skills, while he may have been a technocrat of merit suitable to a bygone era in the '50's, both he and his government lack the drive and the imagination needed to face this problem in the '60's.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
I do not intend to waste the time of the house with a long historial survey or a long historical treatise. But in 1957 when our party came to power-and I am not laying blame on the government or on this side of
[Mr. Grafftey.J
the house-we had to deal with a very serious problem, namely, the problem of unemployment. And in a partisan way I am not going to suggest for one single moment that we completely and entirely solved the problem It was a difficult problem to solve, but I do say that the imaginative government of that day at least addressed itself to the problem of unemployment.
I well remember that when I came into this house in 1958 members of the opposition front bench, including the now Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) and the now Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), legitimately day after day berated the government of that time on the questions of unemployment and employment. We addressed ourselves to that problem and I say to the members of the government, you must address yourselves to the problem of rising costs and inflation. Partisan surveys like the one given yesterday by the Minister of Finance will not be an answer to this problem and will neither be satisfactory to the members of this house nor to the people of Canada.
How did we address ourselves to the problem of unemployment in 1957 and 1958? Our approach in part included winter works, improvement of our national placement service office facilities, increased export sales abroad, the building of technical and vocational schools, and winter "Do It Now" campaigns. These are just a few of the things we initiated which I believe helped in part, but not entirely, to solve the problem of the day. Instead of engaging in partisan attacks on my leader and on our past record I say to the minister and his government, do not wait for the budget, a budget encompassing tax plans. I hope that before the vote is taken this evening a member of the government or one of the government supporters will stand up and tell us at least one concrete plan they have developed in order to face up to this situation, because up to now we have heard nothing.
I say again to the government that we had to face up to the problem of unemployment and I tell the members of the government that they must face up to the problem of rising costs and inflation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I apologize to the hon. gentleman.

Yesterday the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) made some positive suggestions on how we might tackle the problem of rising costs and inflation. I intend, sir, in my brief remarks this afternoon to make some more. When the Leader of the Opposition criticized the government for spending-I think I am paraphrasing his remarks correctly-I do not think he was necessarily criticizing the quantity of the government's expenditures. What he was criticizing primarily was waste, duplication and lack of co-ordination in its spending and the lack of planning priorities with the provinces.
I think we all agree in this house that modern governments must and should spend money if the public sector of the economy is going to keep up with the private sector. We who are responsible for the public sector of the economy must play our part. We must spend more on research. We must spend more on hospitals, on education, urban development and redevelopment, housing and rehousing plans, parks, playgrounds, vocational schools, etc.
Again I say the Leader of the Opposition was not criticizing expenditures for legitimate and logical welfare measures, for education and the like. What we are criticizing is waste, duplication, lack of co-ordination and the lack of planning priorities with provincial authorities.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) and my hon. colleague, the member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), have most ably established already the fact that in 1965 inflation and the rising cost of living constituted a serious problem and continue to be a serious problem today. If we base the index on 1949 as 100, we can see that the average yearly rise amounted to about two points, but between January, 1965 and December, 1965 the index went from 136.9 to 140.8, almost double the average. Who then could contend that inflation is not a serious problem, that rising costs are not a serious problem, and who could contend that we in this house are expecting too much when we ask the government,
Increased Cost of Living before the vote is taken this evening, to tell us at least one or two of its concrete plans in this regard?
I say that this government lacks the determination, the will, the direction and the imagination to deal with this problem in the '60's. The government front bench is filled with experienced technocrats who were perhaps able to conduct the nation's affairs in the '50's, but again I say they lack the imagination to grapple realistically with this problem in the '60's. Sir, unless something drastic happens between now and this evening we can but say and believe that the government has no plans in this regard.
Who in Canada, and I join hands with many members of the N.D.P. who have already spoken in this regard, are primarily affected by a rising cost of living? The answer is simple-the poor, the deprived and the destitute. The hon. lady from Vancouver-Kingsway and my colleague from Edmonton West ably pointed out the fact that when rising costs strike, when inflation strikes, foodstuffs, clothing and housing are affected, and it is the poor, the destitute and the deprived who get it in the neck every time.
Can we sit by, indulging in idle partisan talk and bickering while this situation faces us? I say no, Mr. Speaker. Good times rarely affect the poor, the deprived and the destitute. Prosperity and good times rarely affect them, but I submit that bad times and the remedies usually brought forward to correct them invariably do affect the poor, the destitute and the deprived.
Take as an example, sir, the old classical way of combating inflation and rising prices, a method I do not advocate in its entirety for future application. What happened in the past when governments occasionally moved in the classical sense to combat rising prices and inflation? It was said that government spending had to be cut, and interest rates rose in order to freeze credit. Who got it in the neck every time? It was the poor, the destitute and the deprived. They are watching this parliament, they are looking to this parliament for action and concrete plans and measures. They are not looking to this parliament for partisan historical surveys and bickering.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
We want this government to face up to its responsibilities as we tried to face up to our responsibilities, not always successfully, in respect of unemployment. It is these people living on fixed or shrinking incomes who are largely affected by the problem of inflation

March 22, 1966
Increased Cost of Living and rising costs; it is the old people oi the nation who are so affected. That is the reason my leader and my party have suggested time and time again that instead of talking, discussing and having commission after commission we should raise the old age pension immediately right across the board as we have suggested, because if we wait for a commission to report and on its findings the people who deserve to have a fair share of our national income will be dead before the government acts.
What about poverty in this country? These things have been put on the record before, sir, but I suggest they should be put on the record again because it is the people in conditions of poverty who are affected. Mass poverty is one thing in the African and Asian countries; it is yet another thing in Canada where we have the second highest standard of economic living in the world. Far too many Canadians are not truly sharing in our nation's prosperity today.
Right here at home we have done a poor job in pushing back the frontiers of poverty and want. I submit that individual and national excellence will be a meaningless concept if millions of Canadians continue to subsist on barely minimal standards and conditions. We shall have to put an end to poverty amidst plenty at home, or what will our answer be to communism abroad? The leader of the New Democratic Party and many members of my party have continually put the following statistics on the record of parliament. The Ontario Federation of Labour tells us that in Canada today we can consider that families of four people with net annual incomes of under $2,000 are living in destitution. Who would not admit that? Further, families of four with net annual incomes of under $3,000 are living in poverty. Who would not admit that? Also, families of four people with net annual incomes of under $4,000 a year are living in deprivation.
With these statistics in mind I submit that over 30 per cent of the population of Canada is living in either poverty, deprivation or destitution, and these are the people primarily affected by inflation and rising costs. I think I have shared the experience of many members. Many of the people who daily come into my office in my constituency are the silent, voiceless poor. These are the people who never come under the aegis of private or public welfare help, and it is to the problems of these people that we must direct ourselves in this debate. Invariably these people never

have been in an unemployment insurance office. They would not know what an unemployment insurance book or an unemployment insurance stamp looks like.
What does a prosperous Canada mean to so many people living in poverty? As I said before, let us not have the effrontery in this House of Commons to quote statistics to them. The hon. lady last night well said what effrontery it is to people who are living in poverty amongst plenty to have Dominion Bureau of Statistics figures continually quoted to them. These people are individuals. In fact, very often an ever-increasing gross national product locks more people into grinding poverty.
Today our rising gross national product means that many Canadians are becoming richer while more than 4 million are becoming poorer. Four fifths of us earn salaries or have incomes tied to rising production while the other one-fifth pays for the higher prices with shrinking incomes. I think that this in part is the crux of our debate of yesterday and today; in other words, as a free country we are going to have to put a halt to the type of poverty we have at home if we are going to have a meaningful image in the face of communism abroad.
We have already stated that probably we are not going to solve this problem with the old negative, classical approach to rising prices and inflation. If any government, no matter of what political stripe, is really going to tackle the problem of inflation and rising prices it must encourage the notion of what I consider to be individual and national excellence. None has ever remained in the state of constant chaos which has been our misfortune since April 8, 1963. Canadians have now come to realize the inbred ineptitude that plagues the present administration. But even with its stumbling and stupidity there are areas of this nation which continue to prosper. There is no direction, no goal, unless it be to survive from one crisis to the next with an absolute absence of leadership.
We were criticized during our years in office for the establishment of royal commissions to secure background and recommendations on such matters of national importance as banking, taxation, health and transportation. Today the royal commission has been replaced by the inquiry and the subjects of these inquiries leave much to be desired in the minds of most Canadians. What of the royal commission reports now available to the government from those commissions which we established? They sit gathering dust because this government's ineptitude is so complete it cannot guide the ordinary business of this country to its natural conclusion, legislative action.
Today we find the taxpayer being plunged ever deeper in debt. The government is preventing private enterprise from expanding in a desired manner because of its wish to spend and spend and spend in a time of boom, or near boom when it should be withdrawing from the economy to the benefit of private enterprise. The Minister of National Revenue asked the Leader of the Opposition to state what items should be cut from the list of those upon which the government intends to spend money. Well, it is about time this administration started to do some governing itself and ceased to call on the Leader of the Opposition to give direction.
I say it would be much better for everybody in Canada if the Leader of the Opposition were sitting where the Prime Minister is now so that we could be getting the direction we need in order to go forward in a
March 22, 1966

healthy way. Take my area of Canada, the Atlantic region, where 20 per cent of the unemployment in this nation is found. The Minister of National Revenue would almost lead us to believe that these people are not in existence. I say to him that there are 365,000 people in Canada who are unemployed today. That figure is not from the Martin bureau of statistics; it is from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. No responsible minister in a responsible government would stand up in the House of Commons and brag about the fact that 365,000 people are unemployed. Yet the minister endeavoured to do so by his failure to mention how many people are unemployed in Canada today. Instead, he gave us statistics, and unreliable statistics at that. He said that 3.9 per cent of the labour force were unemployed. Yet the February issue of The Labour Force says that 5 per cent are unemployed. I do not know what to believe.
I do.

I think we will rely on the Dominion Bureau of Statistics rather than on the Minister of National Revenue, though he is a chartered accountant and all the rest of it. Out of those 365,000 I might point out that
65,000	are located in the Atlantic provinces where the unemployment rate is not 3.9 per cent but well over 10 per cent. What is the government doing to reduce this rate or even bring it close to the national average?
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Waiting for suggestions.

Well, it would not make much difference if we made them. Today in the House of Commons when we are debating matters of national importance affecting all Canadians we find only two cabinet ministers present out of a total of 26 or 27. I am not sure how many there are because they have so many new departments and are shifting around all the time. But only one thirteenth of the cabinet is present to listen to the suggestions that are being put forward. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) does not even find it possible to come here when we are debating a subject for which he is responsible.
The 65,000 unemployed in the Atlantic provinces are told that we cannot progress at a faster rate because tight money is in the nation's best interests. The Minister of Finance is unwilling or unable to cope with the special problems of our region. We are the first to feel the effects of a recession and the
Increased Cost of Living last to overcome those effects; yet we are told to sit back and whittle on a block of wood until the rest of the nation overcomes the dangers of the boom period it is now enjoying.
I say to the Minister of Finance that we see no indications of boom in our part of Canada. We see no danger of over-expansion. We see only misery and suffering if special attention is not forthcoming to recognize our special needs in so far as tight money is concerned.
Where is the special attention, so evident during the Diefenbaker years, to our special problems? We are not interested in being grateful to anyone, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) feels we should be, for we do not look upon Ottawa as if we were a beggar but as an area of Canada determined to progress on the basis of sound economic planning that demands recognition from the central authority of our legitimate grievances. Certainly the present rate of unemployment and the tight money policy are not compatible in our area and immediate action should be forthcoming to assist in eliminating both.
What of the cost of living? We earn less and work longer for what we earn in the Atlantic provinces. We have a larger number of pensioners per capita than any other area of Canada. Nowhere is the spiralling cost of living, so evident in our nation today, more crippling than in the Atlantic area. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters), a fellow Nova Scotian, has stated that the government would have liked to increase old age security payments but could not find the revenue. My, that is really touching. It can find $100 million for the C.B.C. every year but it cannot find $100 million to increase old age pensions. What a joke is this statement by the minister. What a miserable joke to perpetrate on those who in many instances are not able to subsist on their present pension cheques. What an irresponsible joke for a government that stands by and watches the cost of living index spiral upwards and by its inaction is taking food out of the mouths of those who need it most.
This is the government we have in Canada today. It is a government so involved with its own inability to govern that it has no time for the problems facing the people. If more ministers would sit in the house when debates are going on they would know more about what is happening in the nation. If they sit in their ivory towers they will never know what is happening to the people of
300G	COMMONS
Increased Cost of Living Canada; yet that is what we see each and every day in this house.
Government ministers are so divided within their ranks that it is impossible to produce a consensus on any given subject. This is what we are told we must live with because the electorate cannot face the thought of another election. Surely, sir, the time will soon arrive when the government will have proven beyond the shadow of any doubt that it is incapable of providing the leadership this nation, approaching its 100th birthday, must have if we are to move forward with national policies that will produce the kind of nation we are capable of being on this North American continent.

Mr. Speaker, the motion and the amendments we are now discussing clearly indicate that the cost of living is rising constantly in Canada.
This state of affairs did not come about in the last few days, or the last two or three weeks. In fact, the cost of living has been rising constantly since the end of the war in 1945. Now, the amendment moved by the Conservatives states: In view of the fact that the cost of living index for the month of February, 1966, reached an all-time high, namely, 142.1 points, this house regrets that the government has failed to act effectively to hold down the cost of living and halt inflation which is having a serious effect on the economy generally and particularly on all people in receipt of social security payments, on war pensioners, old age pensioners, those on fixed incomes, and all low-income groups.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
The situtation was the same, Mr. Speaker, when the Conservatives were in power and they did nothing either in this regard to alter the situation which existed from 1957 to 1962. Why? Surely not because some Conservative ministers did not sincerely want to change the situation. And today, if nothing is being done, it is not that the ministers are not willing to halt inflation and the rise in the cost of living. The ministers today cannot, like those of yesterday could not, I think, halt inflation and hold down the cost of living.
As long as our financial system remains the same, a system which prevails in the public administration of Canadian affairs on the federal, provincial, municipal and school levels, we shall never halt inflation or hold down the cost of living. The system itself produces inflation. Money created by a private system
[Mr. Coates.3
DEBATES	March 22, 1966
commands that money or credit shall end up larger than when created. Such a system involves the germs and the factors of inflation and rise in the cost of living.
The Conservatives, as well as the Liberals, do not want to realize that it is so. Yes, they realize it, but they do not want to say so in the face of the public. The only organization in Canada which is presently prosperous is the financial organization. The financial sharks and leaches benefit from the situation the year round and constantly. The people pay the piper. The people must pay the bills presented by the financiers.
The other organization enjoying some prosperity is the Canadian parliament, because it has the means to practise vandalism, to rob workers, farmers, all the social classes, professionals, manufacturers and small businessmen. It increases taxes or levies new taxes. In fact, Mr. Speaker, since the end of the war, have we not seen fantastic increases in taxes and new taxes in Canada: federal taxes, increase in the income tax, provincial taxes, taxes here and there, school taxes which were increased recently, municipal taxes, all sorts of new taxes, which promote inflation and prevent holding down the cost of living.
Recently, in the Hull area, was there not a strike by teachers? They were striking against the school board, against themselves in fact. They got an increase in salary but the next day, the school tax was increased by 50 cents per $100. When will this increase in taxes end? Taxes contribute to inflation and to the rise in the cost of living.
The amendment moved by the New Democratic party says this:

and this House further regrets that the Government has not established a Prices Review Board to determine the extent to which price increases are unjustified and to take appropriate steps to reduce such prices accordingly.

That means, in plain French, that members of the New Democratic party are in favour of the establishment of a price control commission, such as we had during the war in 1942, 1943 and 1944.
Mr. Speaker, price control means control of wages and production, control of consumption and of the individual. That is why when the vote is taken tonight, we shall vote against the inconsistencies of the New Democratic or Canadian socialist party.
March 22, 1966

Mr. Speaker, they certainly advocate an incentive to the black market. When the C.C.F. or N.D.P. says that during the war, we benefited from the price control board I say -and I know it personally-that there was a black market in Canada at that time. One could get goods with the small coupons of the government that did not take into consideration the needs of the human being and the population in general. Moreover, thanks to those buying stamps, those small coupons, we could get on the black market, provided we paid more, any kind of goods we wished. That is the policy the members of the New Democratic party would like to introduce at present in Canada. Mr. Speaker, that does not work with the Canadian people and the members of the New Democratic party know it.
The old C.C.F. party is looking for it.
Not in Quebec.
No, not in Quebec, nor in any other place. They have changed their program about 15 times in 10 years. They do not know where they are going.
They have changed their program.

Mr. Speaker, as long as our present system will be respected, adulated and even idolized by some people, it will be impossible to hold down the cost of living and to check inflation. When salaries are increased, the higher salaries raise the cost price of goods. I am in the automobile business and I have mechanics working for me. If I pay them $2.25 an hour and charge a customer $4.00 an hour for labour, in short, if I must raise the salary of my employees by 50 cents an hour, naturally, I shall have to charge 50 or perhaps 75 cents an hour more to the customer or consumer who requires the services of my establishment. This is quite understandable.
A business or anything else is run that way. Salaries are included in the cost price of goods. When salaries are increased by 25 to 50 cents an hour and if the retail price of an item goes up by 60 or 65 cents, then the people do not have more purchasing power, but there is inflation, indeed.
What is the cause of this inflation? The system which always requires the industrialist, the businessman, the employer to make
Increased Cost of Living decisions or raise salaries and, by the same token, increase his production costs.
Mr. Speaker, it is exactly like a cat running after its tail. It runs in circles all the time. A price increase results in a salary increase, and so on. We have been going around in circles like this for almost 25 years, since the end of the war.
Mr. Speaker, I was listening a while ago to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) saying that the Conservatives had made no suggestions, and that is a fact. It is all very well to say: cut the expenses. Why did they not cut the expenses when they were in power? And the present government offers no suggestions either. They attack each other, one claiming the other did no better when in power and the other saying: When we were in power, we tried to do better than you. Finally neither one does any better than the other. They are both in the same bag.
The New Democratic party suggests price control. This will still change nothing. It is a poultice on a wooden leg. That is their solution.
The Creditistes, on the other hand, propose to increase the workers' and the Canadian people's incomes without letting this increase be absorbed into the cost of products, without increasing the salaries included in the operating costs.
The Creditistes propose an increase in purchasing power that would not be absorbed into the cost of the goods. Then we have a true increase in purchasing power. By what means? We are suggesting a new way of doing it: compensated consumer discount, so that the consumer can secure an increased purchasing power through a discount at the store where he buys his goods.
The second method, or second proposition: the distribution of a national dividend to every Canadian citizen. Not a dividend based on the moon, no. Not a dividend based on nothing, as the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Marchand) was pleased to claim on television, no. But a dividend based on the actual production in Canada.
Everyone admits that this year the gross national production will be worth over $50 billion and everyone knows, at the same time, that our national income, for the same period, will reach approximately $37 billion. There is a discrepancy between the total production made by Canadians and the income earned by Canadians. There is a discrepancy of $13 billion. Thirteen billion dollars to enable

March 22, 1966
Increased Cost of Living Canadian citizens to buy the existing products, and that amount does not exist. I see that my hon. friend from Matapedia-Matane (Mr. Tremblay) is shaking his head. All the same, it is true that there is a discrepancy of $13 billion between the production and the purchasing power, the people's income.
If you take into account the speed with which money changes hands, supposing that it stands at 2.4 per cent, then you can say that with $6.5 billion you could balance the purchasing power with the real production in Canada.
But it must be done and no action is taken. Instead of cutting into the system, they are trying to cut into the individuals, the contractors, the industrialists, everywhere, all the social classes, instead of cutting into the financial circles which are responsible for the present situation in Canada. They cut into the citizens, the people who are building Canada instead of those who are destroying it.
When the Creditistes talk about a national dividend, they are shocked. A national dividend distributed by the provinces, Great Britain, Jamaica, in short everywhere in the world, that is all right. But the distribution of a national dividend to the Canadian people, who are building Canada, that cannot be done.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
Sheer nonsense.

Like my hon. friend at the other end on this side, he looks just like nonsense.

Mr. Speaker, what are the solutions advocated by the Conservatives, and particularly by the hon. member who just said that is nonsense? Make concrete proposals and we will support them wholeheartedly. We are not narrow-minded like you. Our minds are open to new ideas, but come to us with something new, not always with the same old stories, the same old excuses: there is no money, nothing can be done because no credit is available. Canadians are asked not to invest in the United States because the United States no longer wants to invest in Canada.
The discount rate of the Bank of Canada is increased. How? Do you think that increasing the discount rate of the Bank of Canada will fight inflation in the country, when people have to pay more in interest? Do you believe 
that we are going to fight, slow down or halt the rising cost of living with the increase in the discount rate of the Bank of Canada? The Creditistes suggest the immediate establishment of a national credit commission, made up of experts-I would not even see any objection to the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane being appointed to a position on that commision-study the facts, the true data on the Canadian economy and prepare something which could balance the economy of our nation.
Mr. Speaker, we suggest the creation of a national credit commission which shall make sure, at all times, that the Canadian people will have a purchasing power large enough to buy the Canadian production, that such production will serve the consumers.
Here you will say to me: What about our imports and exports? This changes nothing in the problem, for we are seeking, through all possible means, to export as much as we import-which is quite natural-so that we can have, as much as possible, favourable balances of payments.
Now, this changes absolutely nothing to the solution advocated by the Creditistes, which is that the Canadian public should always have enough purchasing power to buy the products made by the Canadian people, including products exchanged with other countries of the world. Everything is included in that national production.
Mr. Speaker, although the dividend solution is not accepted, nothing keeps the Creditistes from continuing to explain the logic of that solution to the nation as a whole.
Some day members of parliament who will not look at the true solutions to the present economic problems will be replaced by others who will consider such in depth. There is no other way, because at this time, we are getting deeper and deeper into taxes and unpayable debts.
The other day, my colleague from Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) said that the federal government could never pay off its national debt. And that is true. Our municipalities will never be able to pay off their debts. Neither will the provinces, except Alberta and British Columbia; but the other provinces do not follow their example. School boards and individuals are in the same situation.
This system is basically wrong. Take for example the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, which assists in the construction of houses. As you know, there is at present
March 22, 1966

an 11 per cent tax on building materials, which further raises the price of houses.
I shall take my own case as an example.
In 1963, as we sit all year long, I buy a little house in Hull, not through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation but through the Mutual Life Insurance Company. The contract stipulates monthly payments of $88. That is in 1963. When municipal and school taxes are added, my monthly bill is $114 instead of $88. That is for the monthly payment on the house plus the taxes. After three years, my monthly payments are now $132. According to the statement of account for the past year which I received last week, I paid $1,534 to the Mutural Life Insurance Company, including $810 in interest, $510 in taxes and $200 and some odd dollars on the capital. That was for last year.
Would the caisse populaire not have done better?

My hon. friend from Mercier (Mr. Boulanger) asks me whether the caisse populaire would not have done better. Mr. Speaker, a member of Parliament may perhaps cope with such increases, but think of the ordinary labourer, the Hull or Ottawa carpenter, the Noranda miner who buys a little house through the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, having read newspaper advertisements which proclaim: Buy a lovely little house, own your home for just $85 a month.
Mr. Speaker, a worker, a miner, a labourer buys a house, using all the savings accumulated during 15 or 20 years of work, and becomes a property owner, but four or five years later, he finds himself in trouble because the monthly payment goes up following an increase in the school and municipal taxes, and instead of $85 a month, he has to pay back $125 or $130, and then he is forced to put his house up for sale. That is why we see today in many cities in Canada, and particularly in the province of Quebec, workers fighting a system which makes them lose the savings they accumulated during 15, 20 or 25 years of work.
Mr. Speaker, that system cannot go on much longer; it cannot continue with impunity to exploit the masses, the farmers and all social classes.
That is why I urge the Liberal government, the ministers concerned, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) or the Minister of National Revenue to give Canada a financial system
Increased Cost of Living which will reflect the real growth of Canada in the economic, political and social fields and will make it possible to see in our monetary system the real things the Canadian people are asking for.
If the evil lies in the financial system, it should be corrected. And that is where the evil lies when a school which costs $200,000 must be paid back at the rate of $300,000 or $325,000.
Mr. Speaker, it is pure and simple inflation when a little house worth $13,000 costs $28,000, $29,000 or $30,000 when it is finally paid for. Therefore, let us correct what must be corrected, namely the financial system. Let us break the financial shackles which bind the people. Let us not be afraid to throw light on those who exploit the people, who prevent the production and the consumer goods from reaching the consumers in order to set up in our country neither inflation, nor price control, nor something which does not make sense, but a balance between the production of Canadians and their purchasing power.
Then, Mr. Speaker, we would be able to say that we have in Canada a system of economic, political and social freedom and a sound economic system to serve the private individual.
We do not need a government to control us, but to serve the private individual. Let the government be at the service of the human being and then Canada will grow, not only from an economic standpoint, but from a cultural point of view, in national unity and mutual respect between the various elements of our population.
Then we shall be able to say: Canada is a prosperous country and it is inhabited and developed by prosperous Canadians.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we listened last night with interest to the address of the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) concluding with a motion to the effect that the government has failed to act effectively to hold down the cost of living. As I read his address, and I have read it several times, it appears to me to be a great exercise in inconsistency, with on the one hand a recommendation for increased spending in certain sectors, and on the other a very violent criticism of the policy of this government for spending, spending and more
March 22, 1966

Increased Cost of Living spending. The right hon. gentleman toward the end of his speech said:
The government goes on with its other programs and spends and spends.
I have heard it said that the right hon. gentleman can be compared to the shopkeeper who sells a dozen oranges for 34 cents when he is out of stock but at 74 cents when he has them for sale.
During the course of this debate we have been waiting anxiously for precise recommendations as to the course that hon. members of the opposition would like to see pursued.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: This is the speech of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson).

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
No, this is my own speech. I think it can be pointed out that the primary responsibility for direct control of price movements in normal circumstances, that is in conditions outside of war or extraordinary emergencies, belongs to the governments of the provinces and not to the federal authority. There are certain things, of course, that the federal authority can do which are helpful. I point out only by way of example the current policy for improving the technical training and mobility of workers in industry, which helps to relieve labour bottlenecks. In fact, I think this has gone further with our scientific approach to immigration. Second is the policy assistance in easing the expansion of demand by stretching out the federal construction program and helping the provincial governments to postpone work on some shared-cost programs. This, of course, can be successful only to the extent that it meets with the support of the provincial authorities.
The problems that have been raised by hon. gentlemen in the opposition are of course not peculiar to Canada. Today's Globe and Mail carries an article entitled "Higher Pay, Slow Growth Threaten Inflation, Europe Told". This Associated Press article datelined Geneva says:
Soaring wages and a relatively slow growth rate are threatening western Europe with inflation-
The writer points out:
-hourly industrial earnings in western Europe increased during 1965 by 7.5 to 11 per cent. This compared with a rise of 3 per cent in the United States.
The increase in the consumer price index over the past few months is not unexpected. Hon. members are aware of the supply shortage of meats, for example, which is due to a

variety of causes. One is the increased demand for meat by Canadians and Americans. In the area in which I reside is located the largest cattle export point in Canada and I am aware of some of the factors that have caused an increase in cattle prices.
In addition, the introduction of the Canada and Quebec pension plans have undoubtedly led to a modest increase in costs and prices. I do not wish to go into this matter in detail but anybody who studies the effect of these two plans appreciates that initially they will result in certain modest increases. When the adjustments accompanying the introduction of the pension plans have been completed, they will no longer serve to stimulate higher costs and prices.
I am compelled, by some of the comments made by the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates), who was making comparisons with respect to the performance of this government and the former government, to refer to some of our Canadian economists with respect to conditions prevailing now and those which prevailed a short while ago. I think nearly all hon. members are familiar with the work of Harry G. Johnson, Professor of Economics, University of Chicago, who in 1963 in a book entitled "The Canadian Quandary" said:
-I believe that the outstanding problem of the past five years has been mass unemployment. Second, I believe that the problem of mass unemployment has been seriously aggravated by perverse economic policies ineptly pursued by the Canadian economic policy makers.
When we study his chapter on economic growth and economic policy we see .that Dr. Johnson indicates emphatically that "the past five years have witnessed the development of serious concern about the laggardness of economic growth in the three English-speaking countries of the North Atlantic region-the United Kingdom, the United States, and Canada." Then he says:
In the United States and Canada, slow growth has been associated with other phenomena of economic stagnation-higher average unemployment than was previously considered normal, excess industrial capacity, and weak recoveries from recessions-
He makes a comparison with what prevailed in the United Kingdom until the previous year, which would be 1962-63, and other countries in western Europe. Then he says:
The slow rates of growth realized in these three countries-
March 22. 1966

The United Kingdom, the United States and Canada.
-have been in sharp contrast with the rapid economic growth of Europe in the post-war period, and, for Canada and the United States, with the relatively high growth rates realized in the immediate post-war period.
So now we observe another situation wherein Europe is from a competitive point of view running into some of the burdens of higher costs and particularly higher labour costs. I would submit, Mr. Speaker, that an appreciably rising price level is predominantly a symptom of an economic problem rather than its cause. Those who are concerned with this phenomenon which in loose terms is described as "inflation" should be concerned with moderating and not increasing the rate of growth in demand for goods and services. I seriously ask the question whether the Leader of the Opposition has made any contribution whatsoever to this important economic problem.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
The objective of monetary policy is to promote growth of the economy. Continued strong expansion of demand in the economy is our objective. In each of the past two years total spending on goods and services has risen by almost 10 per cent. Canada has experienced a major wave of capital expenditures by private business and by governments. Such expenditures have risen by more than 15 per cent in each of the last two years. Unemployment has been reduced to historically low levels and operating rates in most industries are now close to capacity.
I want to refer later in my comments to some rather classical comments by Von Ha-berler which were used in 1933 to describe some of the problems of the upswing. These indicate that economists at that time had a clear understanding that the economy in upswing may operate close to its effective capacity and that pressure of demand is likely to overload productive capacity. I think this is the burden of the warning of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp1). Monetary policy has always had to take account of the fact that we must borrow very substantial amounts of capital from financial institutions and markets in the United States if we are to pay for the balance of payments deficit of the size we are currently running. This is not a new phenomenon in Canada. We are well familiar with this pattern of trade. Interest rates in the Unites States have risen sharply in recent months. This puts a special burden on borrowers and presents Canada with a
Increased Cost of Living new, a special problem. It is more difficult for borrowers to find the money that they require and they have to pay higher interest rates. We have essentially a new problem of credit.
When I mention that the total of bank loans outstanding has increased by 16 per cent over the year ended February, 1966, I think we can appreciate this serious problem of our economy undergoing a rapid period of growth. Clarence L. Barber of the University of Manitoba is an economist for whom I have had a lot of respect over the years. He speaks of austerity in 1962 and says:
The source of our current difficulties goes back to the year the Conservatives first came back into power. Although Ottawa completely failed to understand it, Canada in 1957 was just entering a period that called for skilful monetary and fiscal management. The problem was there for any government. Well handled, Canada could have come through the period with flying colours. In fact, after five years of slow growth and a record level of unemployment, we have blundered our way into the present mess.
I think everybody on this side of the house likes to feel that if a Liberal government is capable of doing things it is capable of doing them particularly well in the area of finance. We think back to people like Dunning, Ilsley, Abbott, Harris, Gordon and we think that the name of Sharp is in this tradition. I feel that C. D. Howe made a contribution to our growth that was perhaps exemplary.
All these people were white?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
I am sure I do not understand the hon. member's comment. I continue the quotation:
In 1957 Canada was enjoying-
These are the words of Professor Barber:
-a capital spending boom of record size. The Trans-Canada pipe line was being built. The. St. Lawrence Seaway was under way. Uranium mines and smelters were being rushed to completion. And with the shortages created by Suez there was a great burst of oil and gas exploration on the prairies.
Despite a fall in the volume of capital spending the inflow of capital funds continued at an exceptionally high level. Over the five years, 1957 to 1961, it amounted to $6.3 billion. Both Canadian exporters and manufacturers for the domestic market were hampered by the premium on the Canadian dollar. Our unemployment problem was needlessly aggravated. I do not want to go into the details of what has been described in many other debates as a major financial
March 22, 1966

Increased Cost of Living blunder of the previous administration with respect to the reconversion loan. However, it seems to me, just as the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) indicated a few minutes ago, that there were a variety of objectives, all of which had to be considered together and in concert we now have to assess our targets in Canada in the collective sense. In the United States years ago there was a conviction that a boom could not continue for any considerable period of time. I remember that back in the thirties it was felt in the schools of economics that the upswings and downswings were largely inevitable, that we were simply the victims of this economic phenomenon.
In 1946 there was a difference of attitude, and I think of the very well known John Maynard Keynes of England. An example of a man who has been following along in the tradition of the new Keynsian thinking is Walter W. Heller, who has provided important leadership in the United States. The largest problem facing the new economists is the boom that threatens to get out of hand. We believe that the difference between what the economy could produce with full employment, considered achieved when unemployment is 4 per cent, and what it is actually producing is the growth gap. When there is a growth gap it is our purpose to solve this discrepancy by dramatic and effective means. The goal of the new economics is to close the growth gap and the key weapon is the budget.
I ask hon. gentlemen to listen with patience until we hear from one of the most able men who has ever served a Canadian government, the Minister of Finance, who will present his budget in a few days. The budget has already received an exhaustive consideration by some of the best brains in Canada. In my judgment the Department of Finance is still one of the finest departments existing in any modern country in the world. The new economics means that the government's budget can be in the red, no matter for how long or at what stage of business expansion, so long as the economy's actual production is below what could be produced with full employment. In short, the new economists calculate the country's economic potential and tailor spending and money policies to achieve that potential.
Now, of course, we are all concerned that there is an increase in the cost of goods. This is something that inevitably we must have expected. We could not have had this quality of progress in the past several years without this kind of increase. We find, for example,
[Mr. Matheson.l
that in tobacco and alcohol there has been a modest increase of 1.3 per cent. Food, a basic commodity, had increased in February, 1966, over February, 1965, by 7.1 per cent. We can see that in all commodities there has been an increase of 3.5 per cent. The increase in the cost of services has been 3.3 per cent. There are special items such as car insurance which have affected the picture recently. We find also that such matters as work clothes for men have increased in cost as a result of a very substantial increase in demand. This is not the kind of demand that was indicated a few years ago when the right hon. gentleman was heading the government. The recreation and reading subindex to the cost of living index has moved up by a modest 0.6 per cent.
I remind hon. gentlemen of language which may now sound somewhat classical, but the following was written by Von Ha-berler:
Professor Spiethoff describes the mechanism of the cumulative and self-sustaining process of expansion, which begins to work, after the dead point of the depression has been overcome...
The revival of investment activity generates income and purchasing power. Demand rises, first for capital goods and investment materials (iron, steel, cement, lumber, bricks) and later also for consumption goods. Prices rise, mainly prices of capital goods and investment materials. This stimulates further investment. Profits are made which swell the funds available for investment and provide an important psychological stimulus for further expansion. Thus, like a snowball, prosperity increases rapidly as it proceeds.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
The real question, my hon. friends, is, is it possible that we can continue with the enlightened techniques of modern economics, indefinitely into the upswing, as more and more factors of production are drawn into production and people become more and more enthusiastic, without a smaller increase in output and a large rise in costs. What we have seen in Canada with respect to the steady increases in prices is what one must normally expect for an expanding, growing and developing economy. At the beginning of the expansion part of the increase in capital certainly would have been absorbed by a rise in output and by a turnover of goods and a smaller part by increasing prices. But when full employment is gradually approached this necessarily changes. What is required now is the most thoughtful study and consideration of these problems, and I hope that before this vote is taken there will be some serious contribution to this debate by members of the opposition.
March 22, 1966

Of course we are interested in price movements. I suggest that the main reason we are interested in price movements is that these form the substance of the market economy. I could not quite understand the Conservative party's point of view on this matter. Do the members of that party believe in a market economy or do they not? Do they believe, for instance, that the economy is badly adjusted? Do they believe that there is low growth rate, high unemployment, and a balance of payments deficit? We have some of those problems, it is true. But are the members of that party dissatisfied with the current level of growth? If they are not dissatisfied, are they not prepared to accept what every economist regards-
You have not brought the cost of living down.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: This is, of course, one of the burdens of growth. Goods and even labour become scarcer, and prices have to accommodate to this and tend to rise.
I cannot understand that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank hon. gentlemen for their courtesy and patience. It seems to me that the address of the Minister of Finance admirably summed this up where in his concluding sentences he said, as found on page 2950 of Hansard of March 21, 1966:
Our problem Is not to put a brake on the economy;-
I am sure none of us wants to disagree with that.
Put the brake on the cost of living.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
I continue:
-I suggest-
Put the brake on the cost of living.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
I continue:
-the problem is to see that we do not press too hard on the accelerator and throw the car off the road. Our problem in the future is going to be to keep the expansion going without inflation-
And that is the objective of us all.

Mr. Speaker, we have listened to quite a philosophical dissertation by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson), the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister. There was one matter that I did not get quite clear from his speech. Did he mean that the past years in Canada, to which he referred, have been that bad? I
Increased Cost of Living am not sure. I presume I shall have to wait until I see Hansard to get his real meaning.
The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) apologized to me a few moments ago because he thought he would not be here to hear me speak. Perhaps he will not miss very much except that what I have to say concerns something he said a short while ago.
It seems to me that one of the most important things he said was simply that the reduction in excise tax referred to by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition yesterday did not have to do with excise tax but customs duties. This to me is just nonsensical. The minister went on this vein in his speech. I do not think statements such as this bear the merit of rebuttal.
The minister quoted many figures in an attempt to show that the government of which I had the honour to be a member had done nothing toward the economic well-being of this country. The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates) quoted statistics which certainly refuted any claims the Minister of National Revenue may have made.
The minister stated that the price rise to date is not too serious. I would suggest that he ask all those on a fixed income such as pensioners or retired people as well as farmers caught in the cost-price squeeze and other individuals in this category whether they feel that the rise in prices is not too serious. I am sure that the answer would be very emphatic that the price rise is certainly the most serious in many years in this country's history.
I should like to deal briefly with the contents of the New Democratic party's subamendment which reads as follows:
and this House further regrets that the Government has not established a prices review board to determine the extent to which price increases are unjustified and to take appropriate steps to reduce such prices accordingly.
The subamendment is really in two parts and it is the last part with which I quarrel. It reads:
-to take appropriate steps to reduce such prices accordingly.
To me, sir, this is nonsense. I would also point out that this would be unconstitutional.
The Leader of the Opposition yesterday suggested a meeting between the provinces and the federal government in an effort to bring together representatives of the provinces so that together with the government

March 22, 1966
Increased Cost of Living they could make a concerted attack on inflation. I think this is the only thing that can be done. I do not believe that the suggestion made by the New Democratic party can carry any weight. It is, as I said, unconstitutional. Anything that we could do would only have an effect on businesses under federal control.
I agree with the earlier remarks of the Minister of National Revenue when he said that the subamendment would automatically have the effect of bringing about some sort of wage control. I like the argument of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) but I am afraid that the meat of the subamendment does not live up to that argument.
In passing I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) on the excellent speech she made demonstrating her doctrinaire socialism. I wonder how her colleagues, the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Saltsman) and the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Her-ridge), would view the last part of the subamendment.
Yesterday the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis) spoke at great length and very highly with regard to the automobile agreement. He went on to recommend freer trade in many areas. I wonder just what this means? I should like to refer to some answers given to questions which are found on pages 796 and 798 of Hansard for this session. These answers were given as a result of requests for information concerning the export of automobiles and automobile parts. The Leader of the Opposition also put a question concerning imports and the answer is to be found on page 798 of Hansard.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
I think it would be well to point out that in 1963 there was an adverse balance of trade in automobiles and automobile parts. There were actually imports amounting to $577,-
633,000	and exports of $36,997,000. This leaves an adverse balance of trade in automobiles and in automobile parts of $540,636,000. In 1964 the adverse balance of trade was increased by $45,182,000 to $585,818,000. The picture the government tried to put on the record in response to a question by the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Gray) attempted to show only the increase in exports. But the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) insisted on an answer to his question concerning imports, and the increase in exports I have mentioned certainly does not look so

favorable. In 1964 exports of automobiles and automobile parts amounted to $94,257,000. Imports had jumped from $577 millions to about $680 million leaving a net imbalance in trade of $585,818,000, an increase of $45,182,000.
The answers in Hansard to these questions only cover part of 1965. They were given for nine months so far as exports are concerned and for eight months so far as imports are concerned. In consequence I have to admit I have estimated the exports for the full year simply by developing the figure for three-quarters of the year already given and arriving at the total for the full year on an estimated basis. Since the imports were given on an eight month basis I have done the same with respect to them and simply raised the figures by one half. The estimated figure for exports comes to $160 million. Which is a big increase all along the line, but imports increased to $832 millions. This leaves an adverse balance of trade amounting to $672,-
527,000	on automobiles and automobile parts for 1965 on an estimated basis.
This represents an increase of $86,790,000 over the adverse balance for 1964. So we have a general picture of an increase in the adverse balance of trade in automobiles and parts despite the impression which the answers to the questions on exports attempted to leave.
I will not go into the details but there is another interesting question answered on page 2764 of Hansard. Since the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis) yesterday mentioned the achievements, presumably, of the new Department of Industry, I think it should be pointed out that despite what was said back in the debate when the Department of Industry was set up there have been huge increases in the numbers of employees in the Departments of Industry, Trade and Commerce, and Defence Production. I clearly recall that when we on this side questioned the feasibility of setting up this department we were told that the intention was merely to take part of the Department of Defence Production and some employees from the Department of Trade and Commerce in order to set up this new department.
I am afraid the figures emphasize our warning at that time when we said this was simply another departmental bureaucracy building up, one which would not achieve the results for which it was created. So far as I can see, the result so far is an increasing deficit in the balance of payments. I do not
March 22, 1966

see that anything favorable has been achieved.
The Minister of Finance spoke yesterday in this debate. He said that everything the previous government had done was bad and he indicated that the present government were financial wizards. I think this must make everyone at least snicker a little if not laugh out loud. I ask the minister where he stands on the matter of responsibility. Does he stand with his colleagues along the front benches-I am looking at the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) at the moment-

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: He is the only one there.

What has been his position since he voted in favour of debt free money? If ever there was an irresponsible action by a would-be government it was at that time when members opposite supported a motion from down the line in favour of debt free money. The Minister of Finance stands among those hon. gentlemen today and therefore I can only assume that he too would have voted for debt free money as did his predecessor in office. To me this was a completely irresponsible action.
In his remarks yesterday the minister did not indicate that any assistance would be provided for recipients of old age security benefits. What does the government intend to do for these people? The cost of living is spiralling. I know that members of the house and the citizens of Canada appreciate that we on this side did attempt to do something for these individuals, but the present government refused. The minister did not indicate that any help would be forthcoming for farmers caught in the cost-price squeeze.
Others have mentioned this problem. In most areas farm incomes are lower today than they were in 1951, and we all know how costs have skyrocketed. I know the difficulties which these farmers face. If something is not done to help them meet these inflationary prices the situation will soon be out of hand. I can only say that something has to be done.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
The minister did not tell us yesterday what he intends to do about tight money. What about the situation of the small businessman or the small operator right now? I have in mind one case which came to my attention about ten days ago. Application was made to a bank manager for a loan. It was well secured and an excellent risk. The applicant asked for a loan additional to an amount he
Increased Cost of Living already had. The branch manager recommended it wholeheartedly. As I say, it was well secured. However, the word the manager got back was no, that the loan could not be increased under any circumstances, and this gentleman had to go elsewhere. He got his loan and, as I mentioned, it was well secured. He had excellent credit, but he had to pay a higher rate of interest than he would have paid to the bank. This can only be as the result of a tight money policy. It is something which is happening all across the country and the government has failed to act.
The Minister of Finance did not say anything to encourage consumers. Yesterday the Leader of the Opposition pointed out that the price of dressed carcasses of pork during the past few weeks had dropped from 45 cents a pound to 32 cents a pound and yet consumer prices continue to rise. There has been no relief for the consumer in that particular instance. The minister did not say anything about relief from the 11 per cent sales tax on machinery, equipment, building supplies and materials. On August 2, 1963, the minister spoke in favour of this tax. Apparently he is still in favour of it. Apparently we are going to get no relief from it although its elimination could put a halt to the spiralling cost of living.
Several hon. members have quoted statistics during this debate. I am not going to give any more than I have already mentioned in connection with the increased imbalance in trade in automobiles and automobile parts, but I think the 11 per cent sales tax is probably the most important factor in our increasing cost of living. Because building supplies and materials are affected it means that the cost of slight or major repair jobs is tremendously increased. Because machinery and equipment are affected the cost of everything that is produced in factories, including food products, is affected. If one wants to buy a new piece of machinery to produce articles more economically the 11 per cent sales tax has to be paid on the machinery and this increases the cost of the articles. This tax is affecting the cost of everything we export from Canada.
Yesterday the Minister of Finance said that the Leader of the Opposition had exaggerated everything during the course of his speech. I suggest there were many exaggerations by the Minister of Finance. Harking back to 1962, the Minister of Finance said that the Prime Minister had not criticized devaluation of the dollar but the manner in which

March 22, 1966
Increased Cost of Living devaluation had been carried out. I say that the Prime Minister did criticize devaluation all through the election campaign that followed and also in this house. Liberal spokesmen talked about how everything we purchase would cost more. I recall seeing advertisements during that election campaign reading, "Here is what you are paying now; here is what you will have to pay with devaluation."
But the Liberals have done nothing about it since they took office. They accepted that it was the best thing to do. I claim that the upturn swing in the business cycle of this country commenced in 1961.
Hear, hear.

Members of the Liberal party would have us believe that it started in June, 1963. What utter nonsense. There is much well-founded proof to support us in this matter. I suggest to the minister that he look at the record of the Liberal government prior to 1957, which was a do-nothing, standpat government. When we took over it took some time to get this country out of the doldrums in which they left it.
In this connection I should like to quote one statement by the governor of the Bank of Canada from his last annual report:
As the economy moved toward the completion of its fifth year of expansion-
As the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) suggests, I will even do the arithmetic for the minister. Five from 66 is 61. It was in 1961 that the upturn started.
Hear, hear.

I read now from the Commercial Letter of the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce for May-June 1964:
The expansion phase of the current business cycle had lasted three years by the end of the first quarter of 1964.
Three from 64 is 61. It was 1961 when it started.
Hear, hear.

I quote another excerpt:
Most of the primary stimulus during the current expansion has been provided by the external sector, especially since mid-1961 when the efforts to bring about exchange rate devaluation commenced.
Hear, hear.

It is evident that the things done by the previous Conservative government to stimulate the economy began to take

effect in 1961 and I am sure the most important was the devaluation of the dollar at 92J cents. The Liberals discredited that step, but what have they done? They have maintained it.
The Minister of Finance admits that his problems are serious. As he said, he wants to keep the expansion going and not put on the brake but rather ease up on acceleration. But he did not put forth one positive proposal to help these people for whom we are attempting to get something done. I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

THE INCREASED COST OF LIVING Mr. Monteith: Mr. Speaker, at the time the six o'clock recess was called I had been pointing out that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) this afternoon claimed that the government of which I have the
March 22, 1966

honour to be a member, the previous government, had done nothing. I would like to reiterate what I had said before the dinner recess. I would suggest that the minister look back over the actual happenings in respect of what took place in that period.
When we came into power in 1957, we took over from a government which had done nothing, which had been a do-nothing government.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE

speechtext: And still will not.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE
